cases.title: Kryptos K4
cases.summary: Unsolved. Plaintext recovered: 0 percent. 22 of 33 hypothesis families listed (67 percent) are excluded by a count or excluded by the clues; 4 are open. Reviewed through 2026-10-19.
cases.caveat: Progress here means ruling cipher models out against the artist's disclosed clues, fitting one clue and holding the other back. The plaintext is reported to sit in a private archive sold in November 2025, and the custodian still lists K4 as unsolved; the question here is a public method, not whether anyone knows the answer. The share is of the families listed, not of every cipher.
cases.problem: Public cryptanalytic method not established by the checked sources; private archival knowledge documented

lay.tagline: The last unsolved panel of a sculpture outside CIA headquarters.
lay.summary: Kryptos is a sculpture unveiled at CIA headquarters in 1990. Three of its four enciphered panels were read in the 1990s; the fourth, 97 letters long, has never been publicly solved. The artist has released a few words of the answer and where they sit. We use one of those clues to fit a cipher and keep the other back to check it, so a cipher that only fits by luck is caught.
lay.what_it_is: K4 is 97 capital letters on a copper sheet. Jim Sanborn, the artist, has said that the letters at certain positions spell EASTNORTHEAST and BERLINCLOCK. Any proposed method must turn the 97 letters into a text with those words in exactly those places.
lay.what_we_found: Every cipher model we searched to completion either cannot place the clues at all or, when its key is fully pinned down by one clue, gets the other clue wrong. 888 complete keys from layered Vigenere, autokey and Beaufort models with column shuffles all failed the held-back clue. Some partial keys are still undecided.
lay.whats_next: Only add a new cipher model when there is a reason the artist could have used it, fix the clue positions before fitting, and keep one clue for checking. The artist's archive and the custodian's answer checker are private; a matching answer from them would be a reference, not a method.

faq.a: Not publicly. An archive with the plaintext was auctioned in November 2025, and the new custodian runs a private answer checker, but no full method has been published in the sources we checked.

faq.q: Why not just try every cipher?
faq.a: With only 97 letters, many wrong keys can produce a few English-looking words. Holding one clue back is how we tell a real fit from a lucky one.

researcher.summary: 97-letter K4 (ASCII SHA-256 eea81357...). Clues fitted and reserved in reciprocal folds: EASTNORTHEAST at zero-based plaintext offset 21 and BERLINCLOCK at 63. A reserved exact prediction requires a complete key and every reserved letter equal. Completed spaces: ragged columnar (widths to 32, both read orders, A-Z and KRYPTOS alphabets) composed either side of repeating, plaintext-autokey, ciphertext-autokey and Beaufort substitution at periods to 32 (65,024 hypotheses), 0 reserved exact predictions. The Gromark family opened by the family prior is closed in place: any one-alphabet digit key (either sense, any stream) and Periodic Gromark with any keyword at head lengths 2 to 9 are excluded by a digit bound and by SAT over relaxed supersets, cross-checked by exhaustive enumeration at head lengths 2 and 3 and planted controls. Letter chains over letters (mod 26) are settled exactly where the chain still binds: every lag pair at primer lengths 2 to 9, and at 10 every lag pair but (8, 10), by Gaussian elimination over the primer cross-checked by SAT, with the first models appearing at primer length 11 (12 for the subtract recurrence).

families.family: Is it a simple cipher of a known language?
families.evidence: First measurement 20 October 2026: the declared substitution screen (one-to-one substitution with carried word divisions, the alphabet's cipher symbols inside the file's most frequent glyph characters up to 26 plus the word-boundary mark, add-one bigram scoring, greedy swap search with 16 seeded restarts, plants and floors per cell) against two frozen reference proeses, English (Pride and Prejudice, Gutenberg 1342) and Latin (Augustinus Confessiones, Gutenberg 33849). All six (file, language) cells scored indeterminate per the declared rule: real best sits 0.11 to 0.31 nats per counted pair below plant self-parity and 1.17 to 1.33 nats per counted pair above its own destroyed-adjacency floors, consistent across ZL, GC and IT. Plants reached parity exactly 20 of 20 times, so the machinery recognizes a substitution when the material is one; the self-calibrated plant band cannot yet exclude a member of the class scored cross-reference, which is precisely the declared next instrument (a second reference prose per language for a cross-text calibration band). Not covered by this unit: homophonic or polyalphabetic substitution, word-level ciphers, transpositions, nulls, abbreviations. No mapping is published; nothing here is a reading.
families.next: Cross-text calibration: declare a second reference prose per language, measure the cross-text plant band with the same machinery, and only then read the real text's position against the band it should fall in if it is a member of the declared class. If the class survives at bigram resolution, declare a trigram-resolution pass before any wider claim.

families.family: Do the statistics survive a change of transcription?
families.evidence: Measured 20 October 2026 on the 5,013 worded loci shared by ZL 3b and IT 2a outside ten reserved whole folios. Spearman rank correlation over shared types: glyph frequency 0.999, bigrams 0.965, trigrams 0.937, quadgrams 0.915, word tokens 0.901. Glyph totals match within 218 of 184,310; the files split 34,354 and 36,441 tokens (6.1 percent), so the residue is segmentation, not the statistics. Controls: the within-file half-split resampling baseline is 0.73 for word tokens and 0.84 to 1.00 for the rest, so the cross-transcription agreement is at or above the metric's own ceiling; a planted cyclic relabelling of the ten most frequent EVA characters of IT drops bigram agreement to 0.40, trigrams to 0.10, quadgrams to -0.07 and words to 0.26, margins of 0.56 or more; planted miniature files control the pipeline itself. Nothing follows about language or meaning.

families.family: Do they survive a change of word segmentation?
families.evidence: Measured 20 October 2026 on the same 5,013 worded shared loci under two declared segmentations: the frozen long-word convention (delegated to the frozen parser and locked to it on every locus of all three files) and the identical normalisation with every uncertain space cut as definite. IT carries no uncertain spaces, so its two policies agree exactly: a built-in zero-join control. ZL has 2,603 joins: tokens 34,354 to 36,957, the delta exactly the join count; word types fall 8,988 to 7,959 (splitting recycles joined hapaxes, so a large share of measured vocabulary size is segmentation); mean length 5.365 to 4.987. GC behaves the same with 2,321 joins. Sign frequencies are exactly invariant (delta 0 in every file). Word-frequency ranks move to rho 0.942 (ZL) and 0.947 (GC) between their own two policies, not collapse. Cross-file ZL-IT agreement holds at 0.90 or better at every order under both policies, and the split values are all at or above the long-word values (word tokens 0.901 to 0.915), so family 1's conclusion does not depend on segmentation. Planted synthetic loci reproduce the exact token-delta identity. No reading and no language claim.

families.family: Does the text predict unseen folios better than shuffled text?
families.evidence: Measured 20 October 2026 under pre-declared statistics, nulls, seeds and verdict rules. Ten whole folios reserved statistics-blind (f87r, f96v, f95r2, f68v1, f32v, f106r, f67r1, f36r, f82v, f24r) were scored against 1,000 seeded permutations per cell in three files of independent authorship: every cell's real statistic sat below all 1,000 null values, p 0.0010, the budget's floor. Within-word glyph-order structure transferred at 30 to 39 percent below the null floor; word-adjacency structure transferred weakly but beyond all noise at 0.5 to 0.8 percent below the null floor, so most transferable structure lives inside words. Machinery power demonstrated in both directions on planted synthetic corpora; stored null heads and real statistics recompute exactly from the declared per-replicate seeds. This is a necessary condition for language-like structure, not a sufficient one; no language, cipher or meaning conclusion follows. The reservation's testing role is discharged; family 4 must declare its own held-out discipline.

lay.tagline: A 15th-century illustrated book in a script nobody can read.
lay.summary: The Voynich manuscript is a book of about 240 pages held at Yale, written in an unknown script and full of drawings of plants, stars and bathing figures. Its vellum has been carbon dated to the early 1400s. Nobody knows whether it hides a real language, a cipher or no meaning at all. We have not proposed a reading. The plan is to measure first how much the statistics change when you change how the script is transcribed.
lay.what_it_is: The script uses perhaps 20 to 30 distinct signs, written in what look like words. Researchers turn it into Roman letters using schemes such as EVA, but those letters are labels for shapes, not sounds, and different schemes split the signs differently.
lay.what_we_found: Three of four structural questions are measured and the first cipher-shaped test is now in. The declared statistics survive both transcription choice and word segmentation (glyph frequency agreement 0.999; sign frequencies exactly invariant under every segmentation). The held-out test answered yes: unseen folios are predicted better than every one of 1,000 declared shuffles, with the transferable structure concentrating inside words. The substitution screen's first pass is indeterminate by its own declared rule: under the declared search, no relabelling of the text reached the reference proeses' substitution parity (0.11 to 0.31 nats per pair below it), yet the text stood 1.17 to 1.33 nats per pair above its own destroyed-adjacency floors, and the machinery reached parity on all 20 of 20 plants. Cross-text calibration is the declared next instrument. No conclusion about language or meaning is drawn.
lay.whats_next: Family 4's cross-text calibration: declare a second reference prose per language, measure the cross-text plant band with the same machinery, and read the real text's position against the band a class member would occupy; then any surviving class gets a declared trigram-resolution pass.

faq.q: Has the Voynich manuscript been deciphered?
faq.a: No. Many readings have been announced; none has been shown to work on pages its author did not use to build it.
It is not settled. The vellum is old, but that does not tell us whether the text means anything.

Planned statistics: sign n-grams of orders 1 to 4, token lengths and line-position effects under each declared segmentation, with at most 2,000 seeded nulls preserving word lengths or line lengths, and 10 reserved folios.
methods: Declared substitution screen with plant and floor bands

lay.tagline: The writing of Minoan Crete, readable as sounds but not as a language.
lay.summary: Linear A was used on Minoan Crete from about 1800 to 1450 BC, mostly on clay tablets for keeping accounts. Many of its signs look like signs of the later Linear B, which was deciphered as Greek in 1952, so scholars can pronounce Linear A roughly. But the language behind it is unknown, so the words cannot be understood. We have not proposed a reading. The plan is to test which repeated sign sequences hold up across different find sites.
lay.what_it_is: More than a thousand short inscriptions survive, many only a few signs long. The SigLA database records each sign, its shape and where it was found.
lay.what_we_found: Nothing has been executed for Linear A in this project yet.
lay.whats_next: Take a versioned export of the database, check a sample of it by hand, and see whether patterns found at some sites predict inscriptions from a site held back.

faq.a: Scholars can sound out many signs using Linear B values, but the language is unknown, so the texts are not understood.
There is no accepted evidence that it is. Linear B, which is Greek, is a solved comparison, not proof about Linear A.

researcher.summary: SigLA (Salgarella and Castellan) sign occurrences with GORILA-derived inscription metadata. Planned: at most 300 documents from a versioned export with recorded reuse terms, 30 double-annotated, n-gram orders 1 to 3 with at most 2,000 document-length-preserving permutations, and one find-place reserved before feature selection.

lay.tagline: Short inscriptions from the Indus Valley civilization, unread for a century.
lay.summary: The Indus Valley civilization, in what is now Pakistan and northwest India, left thousands of short inscriptions on seals and tablets from about 2600 to 1900 BC. The average inscription is about five signs long, there is no bilingual text, and the language is unknown. Some scholars doubt it encodes language at all. We have not proposed a reading. The plan is to test whether sign patterns predict missing signs once copies of the same inscription are not counted twice.
lay.what_it_is: Several hundred distinct signs are known. Many seals carry the same text, so a careless count treats one inscription as many.
lay.what_we_found: Nothing has been executed for the Indus signs in this project yet.
lay.whats_next: Group duplicate impressions together, hold back a fifth of the groups, and test whether patterns predict hidden signs better than simple position baselines.

faq.q: Has the Indus script been deciphered?
faq.a: No. Proposed readings exist, but none is accepted, and the inscriptions are very short.
Statistical studies find structure, but structure alone cannot prove a language. It is still debated.

researcher.summary: Following Yadav et al. 2010 (PLoS ONE): n-gram prediction and positional regularity. Planned: a documented reusable concordance or at most 500 hand-checked inscriptions, duplicate and related-artifact grouping before a 20 percent group-level split, n-gram orders 1 to 4 against unigram and start/end baselines, at most 2,000 length-preserving shuffles.

lay.tagline: Carved wooden tablets from Rapa Nui (Easter Island) that nobody can read.
lay.summary: Rongorongo is a script of small carved figures found on about two dozen wooden objects from Rapa Nui. Lines alternate direction, so the tablet is turned upside down at the end of each line. A 2024 study dated the wood of one tablet to before European contact, but the wood could have been carved later. We have not proposed a reading. The plan is first to keep originals, plaster casts and photos of the same object from being counted as separate texts.
lay.what_it_is: Surviving objects are scattered across museums. Some museum records are casts of other objects, which can inflate the apparent corpus.
lay.what_we_found: Nothing has been executed for Rongorongo in this project yet.
lay.whats_next: Build a ledger of every object with its museum number and whether it is an original or a cast, then look for repeated passages across originals only.

faq.a: No. A calendar on one tablet is widely discussed, but the script as a whole is unread.

faq.q: Does old wood prove the writing is old?
faq.a: No. Old wood shows when the tree grew; the carving could be later, as the 2024 study itself notes.

researcher.summary: Ferrara et al. 2024 (Scientific Reports, doi 10.1038/s41598-024-53063-7) for wood dates; British Museum records Oc1903,-.150 (original) and Oc1981,Q.1642 (plaster cast). Planned: an object ledger, two annotators on at most 200 sign occurrences of four originals, and repeated-sequence search (lengths 2 to 8, at most 10,000 pair comparisons) with one whole tablet reserved.

lay.tagline: A clay disc from Bronze Age Crete stamped with signs found nowhere else.
lay.summary: The Phaistos disc is a clay disc about 16 centimetres across, found in 1908 in the palace of Phaistos on Crete. Its 241 signs were pressed in with stamps, in a spiral, on both sides, and grouped into 61 sections. No other text uses the same signs, which makes any reading almost impossible to test. We have not proposed one. The plan is to reconcile the published sign lists first and measure how much any result depends on the disputed signs.
lay.what_it_is: There are 45 distinct signs. Because there is only one object, a reading invented from the disc cannot be checked against a second text.
lay.what_we_found: Nothing has been executed for the Phaistos disc in this project yet.
lay.whats_next: Compare two independent sign transcriptions, freeze a small number of grouping variants, and report how much each disputed sign changes the statistics.

faq.q: Has the Phaistos disc been deciphered?
faq.a: No. Many readings have been proposed; with a single short text none can be confirmed.
That has been argued, but the Heraklion Museum treats it as genuine and the question is not settled here.

researcher.summary: Heraklion Archaeological Museum description: 241 stamped signs in 61 groups on two sides, read from the edge inward. Planned: reconcile two cited annotations against the museum count, freeze at most 12 grouping variants, and compare repeated-group and sign-position statistics with at most 2,000 within-side permutations per statistic.

lay.tagline: Two short ciphers from the Zodiac letters that are still unread.
lay.summary: The Zodiac killer sent several ciphers to newspapers in 1969 and 1970. The long 340-symbol cipher was solved in 2020 and confirmed by the FBI. Two short ones, of 13 and 32 symbols, remain unread. They are too short to have a unique answer under simple substitution, so many readings fit. We have not run these yet; the plan is to measure how many readings fit rather than to pick one.
lay.what_it_is: Z13 is 13 symbols, sent with the claim that it contained the writer's name. Z32 is 32 symbols, sent with a map. With so few symbols, almost any short phrase with the right pattern of repeats can be made to fit.
lay.what_we_found: Nothing has been executed for these ciphers in this project. The solved Z340 is kept separate, as a control to reproduce, not a target.
lay.whats_next: First reproduce the published Z340 solution exactly, as a check of the tools. Then, for Z13 and Z32, count how many readings from a fixed word list fit each one, and publish several, not one.

faq.a: No unique reading is established. Many names and phrases fit 13 symbols, so a fit alone proves nothing.
Yes. Oranchak, Blake and Van Eycke solved Z340 in December 2020, and the FBI confirmed it.

researcher.summary: Status follows the Z340 solvers' account (Oranchak, Blake, Van Eycke, arXiv 2403.17350, sections 5.5 and 8.2): Z13 and Z32 unresolved, with many compatible readings under simple substitution. Planned: exact Z340 replay as a solved control, then bounded pattern-compatible enumeration (at most 10,000 checks, 20 stored witnesses) over a hashed lexicon.

lay.tagline: A note of squiggles Edward Elgar sent a young friend in 1897.
lay.summary: In 1897 the composer Edward Elgar sent Dora Penny a short note of 87 small semicircle symbols. She never read it, and nobody has since. We ran standard letter-substitution searches on a published transcription. They produced several different, conflicting outputs, and tests on known messages of the same length showed the method is not yet strong enough at this length to settle anything.
lay.what_it_is: Each symbol is one, two or three small arcs turned in one of eight directions, which gives 24 possible symbols. That suggests each symbol stands for a letter, but the note is so short that many different messages fit.
lay.what_we_found: Our substitution search read a long known test message perfectly but recovered only 80 of 87 letters of a test message as short as Dorabella, and a looser model only 34 of 87. On the real note, three runs gave three different texts. So the result is undecided, not a failure of the idea.
lay.whats_next: Settle the transcription first: two people should mark every symbol's direction independently, since some are ambiguous. Then improve the search on many short known messages before running the real note again.

faq.q: Has the Dorabella cipher been solved?
faq.a: No reading is accepted. Proposed readings exist, but none has been shown to follow from one fixed method that reproduces every symbol.
It has been suggested, and the 2021 study we rely on tested it. We have not tested music here.

researcher.summary: 87-label transcription from the HistoCrypt 2021 deposit (Hauer, Choi, Sundar, Hindle, Smallwood, Kondrak; Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.4819086). Frequency-rank baseline, bijective annealing (3 seeds) and relaxed homophonic annealing (3 seeds) under one English quadgram model, 336,262 objective operations including controls. Matched-length controls: 80/87 bijective, 34/87 homophonic. Target outputs disagree pairwise at 41, 73 and 82 positions (bijective).

charts.title: How much of a known test message the search got back
charts.caption: Share of letters recovered on known-answer controls. Long controls come back fully; controls as short as Dorabella do not, so a miss on the real note is not evidence against the model.

families.family: A plaintext in another language under a large transposition, or in a language not screened
families.evidence: 98 languages with usable text in Universal Dependencies were screened by letter counts, with Russian under four spellings and Esperanto besides; Latin has the lowest median of all and three times the next rate of close windows, though Estonian matches its single closest window. Every window of 59.8 million letters of Latin needs at least 3 errors. Italian and Latin under a one-to-one key are closed; Latin under columnar transposition at widths 2 to 15 is closed; the grille has no power in any language.
families.next: Search Catalan, Romanian and Latin under a 14-column key and under keyed four-square once a method with power exists; screen further languages.

families.family: 14 by 14 turning grille with a letter key
families.evidence: The compiled search finds 4 of 4 planted grilles with the key given and 0 of 4 with it unknown, and order tests barely tell a grille message from no message (3 of 20; 4 of 12). A grille is a transposition, so under a one-to-one key the letter counts still need at least 8 chosen errors in English and 4 in Latin, and random errors never reach them; a grille stays open mainly with a count-flattening key or an unusual text. A homophonic key cannot flatten the counts either: no English window of 196 letters uses 18 letters or fewer, and no Latin window groups exactly into the cells' 18 symbol counts (the closest needs at most 3 errors). Under the Latin model, with the key held fixed the search recovers 4 of 4 grilles with the true key, 1 of 4 with keys 77 to 82 percent right and 0 of 4 at 65 to 69 percent; re-solving the key at every grille move recovers 0 of 8.
families.next: A joint method that recovers planted grilles with the key unknown, before the cells are searched; the count-flattening key left to test is a pair code or keyed squares, since a homophonic key is excluded by counts.

families.family: No message (a hand construction)
families.evidence: Against random dealings of the cells' own symbols the order gives a family-wise p of 0.28, with a test that flags 19 of 20 keyed-square and done-columnar messages but only 3 of 20 grille messages; a grille-specific statistic has weak power (4 of 12) and the cells sit among their dealings (25 of 40). A message now needs an order-destroying transposition and either a non-homophonic count-flattening key, chosen errors or an unusual text. The five last-column symbols fit neither plain reading: as padding the other 188 cells use 13 letters, fewer than any window of 188 letters of Latin (fewest 14) or English (fewest 19); as real rare letters they would have to cluster where no Latin or English window clusters them.
families.next: Find an order statistic that separates a turning-grille message from a no-message dealing at 196 letters, with planted texts, since the grille is the main message system the order still allows.

families.family: A general pair table (2 by 2 Hill, any 625-pair code)
families.evidence: The different-pair count does not exclude a general pair table; a 2 by 2 Hill matrix drawn at random spreads English over at least 23 symbols (0 of 1,110 draws reach the cells' 18), so random Hill keys are excluded, but a chosen 625-pair table is not.
families.next: Search 2 by 2 Hill over a keyed square with planted texts.

families.family: Transposition beyond the searched widths, or with nulls and an incomplete rectangle
families.evidence: The key-invariant method has no power past width 10; double transposition is closed only to width 6. Latin is closed by searches with Latin power at every width from 2 to 15; English under any transposition with a one-to-one key is already excluded by counts. Under the Latin model a joint search of both orders and the key recovers planted Latin at 4 by 5 and 5 by 7 (6 of 6) but 1 of 3 at 6 by 8 and none at 7 by 9 or 9 by 11.
families.next: A joint search with a letter key above width 15 and for double transposition above width 6, in Latin first, since counts already exclude English under a one-to-one key.

families.family: Four-square with keyed plain squares, and two-square
families.evidence: With chosen plain squares 15 of 15 held-out English windows reach the cells' side counts; a search annealing all four squares recovers 0 of 6 planted texts at 196 letters, so it has no power yet.
families.next: A search with power for keyed squares at 196 letters, for example fixing the Polybius labelling from the cells' structure or using a stronger model, before the cells are searched.

families.evidence: Latin is the closest of 39 languages by letter counts (4 errors at its closest window), but planted Latin comes back 6 of 6, also with 8 slips, and 7 of 8 shuffles reach the cells' best under a Latin model. Word coverage settles heavy errors: with up to 32 wrong cells of 196, 59 of 60 planted Latin texts keep more Latin words than the cells' best decryption (12.8 percent), which 3 of 4 shuffles reach, under the keyed square, the dummy rule and columnar widths 2 to 15.

families.family: Latin under columnar transposition at widths 2 to 13 and 15, with a short last row, and a letter key
families.evidence: 87 of 88 planted Latin texts recovered at widths 2 to 13 and 15, classical and 8-error texts included; the cells score -3.57 to -4.59 a letter, below every recovered planted text and inside their shuffles (at widths 2 to 9, 4 of 32 cases beat all five shuffles, about what chance gives).

families.family: Catalan and Romanian under a one-to-one key, with or without the book's dummy rule and errors
families.evidence: Planted text comes back 3 of 3 in each, also with 8 slips; the cells sit inside their shuffles (Catalan 7 of 8; Romanian 13 of 40 after an edge at 8 shuffles vanished).

families.family: Latin under a repeating coordinate shift, and under four-square with standard plain squares
families.evidence: The shift count does not exclude Latin (1 of 9,774 draws reaches the cells), but the joint search recovers 15 of 18 planted Latin texts and the cells sit with their shuffles; four-square recovers 3 of 3 with the cells inside their shuffles. A capped homophonic key recovers only 2 of 3. At periods 6 and 8 to 13 the search recovers 25 of 28 planted Latin texts and the cells' best, -4.02, sits with their shuffles (7 of 28 cases above all three, as chance gives).

next.family: A plaintext in another language under a large transposition, or in a language not screened
next.next: Search Catalan, Romanian and Latin under a 14-column key and under keyed four-square once a method with power exists; screen further languages.

next.family: 14 by 14 turning grille with a letter key
next.next: A joint method that recovers planted grilles with the key unknown, before the cells are searched; the count-flattening key left to test is a pair code or keyed squares, since a homophonic key is excluded by counts.

next.family: No message (a hand construction)
next.next: Find an order statistic that separates a turning-grille message from a no-message dealing at 196 letters, with planted texts, since the grille is the main message system the order still allows.

next.family: A general pair table (2 by 2 Hill, any 625-pair code)
next.next: Search 2 by 2 Hill over a keyed square with planted texts.

next.family: Transposition beyond the searched widths, or with nulls and an incomplete rectangle
next.next: A joint search with a letter key above width 15 and for double transposition above width 6, in Latin first, since counts already exclude English under a one-to-one key.

next.family: Four-square with keyed plain squares, and two-square
next.next: A search with power for keyed squares at 196 letters, for example fixing the Polybius labelling from the cells' structure or using a stronger model, before the cells are searched.

lay.tagline: A 1939 puzzle that its own author could not, or would not, explain.
lay.summary: In 1939 Alexander d'Agapeyeff printed 392 digits at the back of his book Codes and Ciphers as a challenge. Nobody has ever read them, and later editions quietly dropped the puzzle. We have not read it either. What we have done is rule out most of the ordinary ways it could have been made, using tests we first proved can find a hidden message of the same length.
lay.what_it_is: The digits come in pairs. Each pair names a cell of a 5 by 5 grid of letters, called a Polybius square, so the puzzle is 196 grid cells laid out in a 14 by 14 block. If the grid were simply a letter table, swapping the cells for letters would give a message. It does not: the result reads like random letters in every language tried.
lay.what_we_found: Before trusting a negative result we plant a known message of the same length, encipher it the same way, and check that the search finds it. Searches that pass that test and still find nothing on the real puzzle count as closed. Some ideas are ruled out without any search, because the puzzle's letter counts are impossible for them. Latin fits the letter counts better than any of 98 languages, but Latin searches with shown power also came back empty.
lay.whats_next: Nothing, for now. On 18 October 2026 we closed this research, because we think there was probably never a message. That is an interpretation, not a proof. The biggest idea still open is a turning grille, a card with holes rotated over the page, combined with a second step that evens out the letter counts, and our grille search cannot yet find a planted message, so a grille message is not ruled out. The exclusions and the paper stand as published. If the work reopens, the first job is a grille method that can find a planted message, not more computer time.

faq.q: Has anyone solved the D'Agapeyeff cipher?
faq.a: No reading has been accepted. Several have been published; we checked eight, and none survives the letter counts the cells force, and three fail their own stated method.

Not under any simple system. No window of ordinary English prose has the puzzle's letter counts under a one-to-one letter key, in any order. English is still possible under systems that change the counts, such as a grille plus a second key, or with deliberate errors.

The letter counts point toward Latin, not Russian. Of 98 languages screened, Latin has the lowest typical distance from the cells' counts and three times as many close stretches as any other; among 59.8 million letters of Latin the best 196-letter stretches need only 3 changed cells. Russian needs at least 9 under every transliteration tried, no closer than English. But Latin under the simple systems, and under columnar transposition at widths 10 to 15, was searched and nothing was found, so this is a lead for harder systems, not an answer.
A construction with no message fits every statistic measured so far. That does not prove it is a hoax; the test cannot yet tell a turning grille from no message.

researcher.summary: 196 Polybius cells (row digits 6 to 0, column digits 1 to 5) from the Wikipedia transcription of the 1939 challenge. Exclusions come in two kinds: key-invariant counts (fewest single-cell errors under any one-to-one key equals half the L1 distance between sorted count vectors) and compiled annealing searches whose power is shown on planted held-out texts, with shuffled cells as the control. A no-message null (van Eykelen's recipe) is not rejected: family-wise p 0.28 over thirty order statistics, with power 19 of 20 on keyed-square messages but 3 of 20 on grilles.
methods: Compiled annealing with planted-text power checks
Language screen over 39 Universal Dependencies treebanks
No-message null over thirty order statistics

manuscript.title: Excluding Classical Cipher Families for the 1939 D'Agapeyeff Challenge
manuscript.status: Released as preprint 1.0.0 on 8 October 2026 and archived on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23241304 (every version: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23241303), verified by tools/paper-zenodo-check.py. Four internal readings were done and fixed; seven searches were rerun under a second seed and agree. The companion repository is ChaseHendrick/dagapeyeff. Not peer reviewed.

charts.title: How many cells would have to be wrong for each language to fit
charts.caption: Fewest single-cell errors that turn a 196-letter window of real text into the cells' letter counts, under any one-to-one key and any order. Lower is a closer fit. 98 languages from Universal Dependencies (non-Latin alphabets romanized), English from the 1.9 million letter prose corpus, Russian under its best of four spellings, and Esperanto from ten books.
